turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Thursday, the seventeenth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go. [warmly] Claire, what's on top?
Three things. The Federal Reserve raised rates — the first hike since twenty twenty-three — straight into an oil shock it cannot reach.
The Gulf tips from a stand-off into an open tanker war. And — [excited] — radio-control rock crawling, all the way down.
[wry] Of course it does. Start with the strait, Theo, because the whole book bends around it.
So the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively shut since late winter. What changed this month is that it turned kinetic.
American forces struck three Iranian oil tankers. Iran's Revolutionary Guard had fired ballistic missiles at two US warships first. Tehran claims it hit back.
[thoughtful] And traffic through the strait has basically collapsed.
Roughly eight ships transited on the thirteenth. A normal day is about eighty-five.
Eighty-five down to eight. [exhales] That's a waterway carrying nearly a fifth of the world's seaborne crude, moving a tenth of its ships.
And the tanker that does sail now sails as a target. Brent settled the week near a hundred and seven dollars — a four-month high.
Okay, but here's the part I didn't expect. The first crack in the oil price isn't a supply crack. It's demand.
Right. Both OPEC and the International Energy Agency cut their demand forecasts. A war that has spilled no barrels is running into a demand curve bending the other way.
[curious] So who's actually reading this as a war, and who's reading it as a price?
Three desks, three framings. Al Jazeera calls it a tanker war with no off-ramp. Iranian state media calls it sovereignty — self-defence of Iranian waters.
And the markets desk?

Bloomberg and Reuters treat it as a supply story, not a war story — and they think the rally's overdone. Morgan Stanley sees Brent near seventy-five for the rest of the year. Citi, toward sixty once Hormuz normalises.
[skeptical] Sixty. So the bet is that fear, not shortage, is doing the pricing.
And fear is the part that fades. One more number: China and India together still take about forty-four per cent of the Iranian cargoes moving through the strait. Some under naval escort.
So Asia is quietly keeping it flowing. That's why the physical market hasn't seized even though the map looks like war. [thoughtful] Huh.
Elsewhere, briefly — Europe's eastern airspace keeps getting tested. Romania's counted about thirty-three drone incursions since twenty twenty-two. Copenhagen's airport was closed by drones.
And Gaza?
A ceasefire that holds only in the sense that the killing has slowed. Four Palestinians reported killed on the fifteenth. The word is doing a lot of work.
[sighs] It is. Take me to the money, Claire. The Fed hiked.
The Fed hiked. A quarter-point, to a range of three and three-quarters to four per cent. First rate rise since twenty twenty-three. Unanimous.
Into an oil shock. That's the bit people are arguing about.
The chair, Kevin Warsh, means it. The dot plot is hawkish — sixteen of eighteen officials project at least one more hike this year. Four want two.
[exhales] And the market?

The ten-year Treasury yield touched five per cent — a level unseen since two thousand seven. The dollar had its best day since June. Gold made fresh records. Bitcoin did not — it fell toward a three-week low.
Gold up, bitcoin down, on the same day. Unpack that.
Gold is doing its job as a hedge even against higher yields — the geopolitical and stagflation bid. Bitcoin wears the risk-off tone, plus a failed crypto bill in the US Senate.
[curious] So what does it mean for the boring, sensible portfolio? The all-world fund, the global bonds.

Headwind for both. Higher discount rates and a strong dollar squeeze global equities at once. Global bonds feel the rising yields, though currency hedging cushions it. This is explanation, Theo, not advice.
Noted. And the sceptics — because there are sceptics.
Loud ones, and not on the fringe. Mark Zandi of Moody's says the textbook answer to a supply shock is: don't respond. A strategist calls it a growth shock dressed up as inflation.
[skeptical] So the Fed might be doing efficiently the exact thing it shouldn't do at all.
Which is the line running under the whole issue. Peter Drucker: there is nothing so useless as doing efficiently that which should not be done at all.
[warmly] I love a Drucker morning. Singapore — the haze broke, right?
It broke. A day after the worst air in seven years — the central reading touched a hundred and fifty-four — it fell back into the seventies and eighties.
On what? Policy?
Rain. Showers over Kalimantan. Not the law. And that's the sceptic's whole point — the Transboundary Haze Act has never once carried a prosecution to a conclusion.
[deadpan] A lever that reaches the smoke by waiting for weather.
Exports, meanwhile, rose seven point seven per cent in August. A real electronics recovery, but a hard slowdown from July's twenty-four per cent.
Alright. Silicon and sovereignty. There were — what — five frontier models in ten days?

Five. But the story with a lever attached is quieter. A server subsidiary called Aivres — the American arm of a blacklisted Chinese firm — routed more than five and a half billion dollars of advanced tech into Southeast Asia.
Including the good chips?
Over three billion dollars of Blackwell servers that ultimately served Chinese customers. The parent's been on the blacklist since twenty twenty-three. The subsidiary is not.
[scoffs] So the export wall is a speed bump. The rule named the parent and missed the shadow.
[curious] And the five models — anything a normal person should care about?
Not really. The frontier crown changes hands every few weeks now, and the gaps at the top sit inside the noise of how the tests are run. It's a spectator sport.
So the real news is the plumbing, not the fireworks.

Who controls the distribution, who controls the silicon, and who can run a capable model cheaply enough to own rather than rent. And for the home-lab reader, the thing that actually changes your build this quarter isn't a model. It's memory.
The RAM thing. How bad?
A thirty-two-gigabyte kit that cost around eighty dollars in mid-twenty twenty-five now runs three hundred and seventy-five to five hundred. The fabs are diverting capacity to AI memory.
[gasps] Nearly five times. So buy the RAM now.
Buy the RAM now. The best model you can run at home is Chinese and cheap — a GLM variant, or a Qwen dense model on a single card. The memory is the constraint.
Okay, gear. Sonos put a whole system on your head.
The Ace Ultra. Four hundred and forty-nine dollars, wide availability the twenty-ninth. Adaptive cancelling, about thirty-five hours of battery.
[curious] And the trick?
Hold a button, and the music playing on a nearby Sonos speaker hops into the headphones over Wi-Fi. Then back to the room. The headphones become a node of the system.
That's genuinely clever. What's the catch?

[wry] It's worth exactly nothing if you don't already own the speakers. A walled-garden feature at a price that hasn't moved from the first Ace — and Sonos's app is still recovering from a rough rewrite last year.
Wait it and see. Now — the maker desk. Toothbrushes. [amused] You promised me this would be interesting.
It's the most sceptical desk in the book. Two mechanisms: an Oral-B spins and pulses; a sonic brush vibrates. And exactly two features have the evidence behind them.
Which two?

The pressure sensor and the timer. That's it. The landmark review found powered brushes beat manual by about eleven per cent on gum inflammation — and the authors themselves call the clinical importance unclear.
[skeptical] So the three-hundred-dollar brush with the screen and the app…
Is theatre. The real business is the head. An Oral-B replacement head runs eleven to twelve dollars, four a year — in under two years that alone out-costs a whole rival handle.
The handle's the razor, the heads are the blades.
Exactly. Philips even puts a chip in every head that counts seconds, not wear, and tells you to replace it on a timer. Look at your bristles, not the light.
[laughs] Look at your bristles, not the light. That's the whole desk.
A good manual brush and floss is the honest ceiling. The electric's real case is narrow — it babysits people who brush too hard.
[warmly] Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.

[excited] Radio-control rock crawling and bashing. Two tempers, one obsession. Crawlers pick a slow line over a boulder, inch by inch. Bashers launch a truck off a ramp at fifty and repair what breaks.
And people fall in at a specific moment.

For crawlers, it's the slow-line epiphany — the first time patience and torque put the rig somewhere it looked like it couldn't go. For bashers, it's the first clean backflip. Or surviving a twenty-foot lawn dart with nothing broken.
[amused] A twenty-foot lawn dart.

The subreddit for cars at large runs about a hundred and fifty-eight thousand members. The market's around one and a half billion dollars a year. And here's the buy-once lesson, Claire — skip the toy.
Skip the toy?
The sub-sixty-dollar department-store truck has no parts support. The first thing that breaks ends the hobby. Start one rung up — a hobby-grade micro, around a hundred and ten dollars.
And the first upgrade isn't speed.

It's brass. You bolt machined brass — about eighty-one grams a wheel — low in the chassis to drop the centre of gravity and stop the rollovers. [warmly] It's the least glamorous, most important thing you buy.
And there's a big release the community's excited about, right?

Traxxas teased a one-tenth truck with factory portal axles — geared hubs that lift the axle for clearance, the thing people used to machine in by hand. Most anticipated item of the year in this little world.
[amused] A little world with strong opinions.

The deepest. There's a fault line between scale purists, who want the rig to look like a real truck, and the performance crowd, who'll bolt a low ugly chassis under it just to climb better. They call that a cheater rig.
[curious] And the money pit?

It's real. The community's own honest line: a rig is never finished. On a five-hundred-and-fifty-dollar basher, a round of weekend upgrades runs three to five hundred more. Breakage isn't a risk — it's the business model.
So it's four hobbies in one shell.
Engineering, driving, building, collecting. You arrive for one and stay for the other three. In Singapore you run them at indoor tracks, or a car-park, and the used market on Carousell is alive.
[wry] A room full of lithium packs and machined brass. Noted.
Quick hits on the rest. Screen and Sound — a witch sequel opened number one.

Practical Magic Two. Critics at about a third, audiences past ninety. The widest split of the year. And the sceptic's read is that the ninety measures affection for the nineteen ninety-eight original, not the film in front of you.
A nostalgia score. And the watch desk?
Grand Seiko's most accurate mainspring watch — good to twenty seconds a year — and, finally, the adjustable clasp its owners have begged for. Eleven thousand four hundred dollars, though.
[exhales] And the catch, because there's always a catch.
It's quartz-regulated. So you're paying eleven thousand dollars for battery-free-but-not-purely-mechanical precision. Purists have questions.
The family desk — this one matters to a lot of listeners.
Australia ran the world's first under-sixteen social-media ban. Nine months in, the evaluation is in: usage fell from about eighty-six per cent to eighty-two. That's it.
[thoughtful] Four points.
And between fifteen and nineteen per cent of kids just used fake accounts. The uncomfortable finding: parental awareness of what their children were doing actually fell.
So the ban drove it out of sight.
The lever that works isn't a ban. It's a bedtime. The device merely present in the bedroom worsens a twelve-year-old's sleep even when it's never touched. Charge the phone in the kitchen.
[warmly] Charge it in the kitchen. Simple. And fitness — the walking thing.
A big study found your walking pace out-predicts your cholesterol panel for early death. More than four hundred thousand people.
[curious] Your walking speed beats a blood test?

In people with existing conditions, swapping the blood panel for self-reported walking pace improved the model. But — the sceptic — it's a proxy. Sick people walk slower because they're sick. It's a screening prompt, not a promise.
And the Diary, fast — what do I book?

The Grand Prix, ninth to eleventh of October, with its first-ever Sprint. The Kyushu sumo goes on sale Saturday the nineteenth — the good days vanish in hours. And a four-night stadium run in December.
And where do I eat?
A basement curry the whole island is queueing for — a thirty-six-hour black curry from a stall that grew up out of a university. The pick of the week.
[warmly] A thirty-six-hour curry. Okay. Bring us home, Claire — the long read.
[drawn out] New Zealand. And the argument is: the collapse of the moat.
The moat being distance.
For two centuries, distance was the country's cheapest drug policy — too far, too small for a cartel to bother. That protection is gone.
[thoughtful] And the drug didn't land in the cities.

It settled in the small towns the economy hollowed out. Meth consumption's hitting records — one town's reading quadrupled in a single year. And the price collapsed: a gram fell from about five hundred and sixty New Zealand dollars to three hundred and thirty-four.
So it stopped being an occasional thing.
And became a daily, get-through-the-shift thing. A numbing drug for the economically squeezed. The frame that fits isn't vice. It's despair.
[thoughtful] And the supply — how does it even get there?

Through the gangs. The Comancheros, an Australian outlaw club, set up shop in New Zealand after their senior members were deported from Australia — sent home to a country some had barely lived in, with the networks intact.
[scoffs] So a deportation policy meant to export a problem helped seed one.

The networks came home with the men. And there's a bitter symmetry: the isolation that once kept the drug out is exactly what makes New Zealand a prize now — a small, wealthy, high-price island at the end of a shipping lane.
[sighs] And the state's answer?
Border seizures. And a national advertisement that, by one account, people watched for an average of two seconds before scrolling on.
Two seconds. [scoffs] That's the whole issue, isn't it. Drucker's line.

It is. Because there's a program that works — a Northland partnership on the demand side that reports a thirty-four per cent drop in harm from offending, and three to seven dollars back for every dollar spent.
And it's underfunded.

While the seizures make the news. Efficiency everywhere, aimed at the wrong thing. When the Financial Times writes this up in three weeks, it'll be a story about a small country finding out its oldest defence quietly stopped working.
[drawn out] And the reader of that page knew first. [pause] That's the whole point of the desk.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
